title: Connecting Microseismicity to Lithology via a Model of Slip Avalanches
authors: Ethan A. Mullen, Yanbo Wang, Jordan J. Sickle, Frank W. DelRio, Pania Newell, Anastasia G. Ilgen, Karin A. Dahmen
abstract: Fluid injection into the earth's crust can induce small and frequent earthquakes in the subsurface. Predicting their sizes and temporal occurrences via statistical analysis is crucial for safe operations in unconventional oil and gas recovery, enhanced geothermal systems, and geologic carbon storage. Here we show that a simple micromechanical model of slip avalanches in slowly deforming solids predicts the slip statistics observed over drastically different spatial scales, namely meter-scale microseismic observations and nanometer- to micrometer-scale nanoindentation experiments can be described with this model. Microseismic catalogs extracted from high-pressure fluid injection operations into geological basins with various lithologies and nanoindentation experiments on shale across a wide range of temperatures and mineral compositions yield statistics consistent with model predictions. This universality across materials, temperatures, and scales is consistent with the prediction that the slip statistics result from only a few basic properties. Previously debated deviations of the statistics in layered sedimentary formations are explained by finite-size and stress-integrative effects resulting from mechanically weak bedding planes. The slip statistics therefore provide important information about the structure and scales of the bedding planes. Conversely, the basin structure can also be used to predict the probability distribution for the sizes of triggered microseismic events.
summary: This research develops a micromechanical model of slip avalanches to predict earthquake statistics induced by fluid injection into underground rock formations. By comparing observed event size distributions from both lab nanoindentation tests on shale and real-world microseismic catalogs, the authors demonstrate that these statistics are universal but sensitive enough to reveal the underlying lithological structure of the rock.
main_problem: Predicting the sizes and temporal occurrences of small earthquakes induced by fluid injection into the Earth's crust for safe industrial operations.
main_result: The slip statistics (like the b-value) are universal, depending only on basic properties, and can distinguish between different lithologies (e.g., layered vs. non-layered sedimentary rocks).
method: Comparing observed power-law scaling exponents from microseismic catalogs and nanoindentation experiments against predictions from a mean-field model of slip avalanches.
model_or_system: The study uses a micromechanical model of slip avalanches in slowly deforming solids, applying concepts from statistical physics to analyze event size distributions across vastly different spatial scales (nanometers to meters).
key_observables: Size distribution exponents ($\kappa$ or $\alpha$), the Gutenberg-Richter b-value, and cumulative distribution functions of seismic moments.
important_parameters: Lithology type (layered vs. non-layered), temperature range ($25^\circ	ext{C}$ to $500^\circ	ext{C}$), and material composition (mineralogy).
main_assumptions: The slip statistics are governed by a mean-field theory, which simplifies complex interactions but successfully predicts scaling behavior across materials.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate nanoindentation load/displacement traces on different shale types at various temperatures, and plots show the comparison of microseismic event distributions for sedimentary versus non-sedimentary formations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (induced seismicity hazard), introduces the mean-field model for slip avalanches, applies this model to analyze both nanoindentation data on shale and large-scale microseismic catalogs from different geological settings, concluding that event statistics reveal underlying structural information about the rock.
why_interesting: While applied to geophysics, the core methodology relies heavily on analyzing power-law scaling in non-equilibrium systems (avalanches), which shares mathematical parallels with critical phenomena studied in statistical mechanics and disordered systems.
